newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP adopts zero growth budget for 1997.
newsitem.headline: EP adopts zero growth budget for 1997.

text.p: The European Parliament agreed on Thursday a 1997 European Union budget which achieves zero growth, an unprecedented attempt at spending restraint.
The effort to contain EU spending supports the struggle by national governments to curb their own budgets ahead of Economic and Monetary Union, expected in 1999.

This is the first time the Parliament has approved a budget which is smaller than the one originally proposed by the European Commission, the head of Parliament's budget committee, Detlev Samland, told journalists on Wednesday night.
Overall, the Parliament agreed a budget for 1997 worth 89.14 billion Ecus ($110 billion) in commitments and 82.37 billion Ecus ($102 billion) in payments.
This compares with 1996 commitments of 86.53 billion Ecus ($107 billion) and payments of 81.88 billion Ecus ($101 billion).

Irish Budget Minister Hugh Coveney said after the vote, which concludes the 1997 budget adoption procedure, that the EU Council of Ministers thought the budget was satisfactory because it respected the ceiling ministers had placed on EU spending.
Ireland holds the EU presidency until the end of 1996.
"The outcome is quite satisfactory from the Commission's point of view," EU Budget Commissioner Erkki Liikanen told a news conference on Thursday.

Euro-MPs agreed to a compromise with ministers on financing for European rail and road networks, European research and the peace process in Northern Ireland, for which they originally demanded 300 million Ecus.
In practice, they agreed that 100 million Ecus ($124 million) for Northern Ireland could come from savings in other policies so asto keep the overall payments ceiling untouched.
They also agreed another 100 million Ecus for trans-European networks, the so-called TENs, could be financed from the EU's foreign policy budget, rather than its internal policy coffers.
This means that the money can be used to fund transport links to Central Europe and the countries of the Mediterranean basin, but not for links between EU member states.
The battle over additional money for the TENs has been at the heart of the Commission's plans to spur job creation.
The Commission has argued more money is needed to complete the large infrastructure projects, which include an extension of high speed rail links across Europe.
Parliament accepted a 74-million-Ecu budget for research after ministers promised a further 26 million Ecus could be found in savings from other budget lines.

But there was one major point where the outcome disappointed budget committee president Samland, a Socialist, and Laurens Brinkhorst, the Dutch Liberal who steered the 1997 budget through the EU's directly-elected assembly.

Parliament threatened in September to freeze all financing for Turkey, which Euro-MPs feel has reneged on its promises to improve respect for human rights and democratisation in return for the assembly's approval in December 1995 of an EU-Turkey customs union.
Euro-MPs agreed to freeze the 53 million Ecus ($66 million) promised to Turkey for 1997 to help set up the customs union. This comes from a 1996-2000 package worth 375 million Ecus ($465 million).

But to the disappointment of the rest of the assembly, the Christian Democrats -- Parliament's second largest political group -- refused to support a call to freeze a further 100 million Ecus from the MEDA programme of assistance to the countries of the Mediterranean basin.

The decision came after Commission president Jacques Santer promised the assembly that Turkey would only receive funding from the MEDA programme for projects designed to support respect for human rights, democratisation and civil society.
